title: When Muslims let you down
hook: Someone at the masjid was harsh, or cold, or just plain rude. It hurts. It isn't Islam.

screens.text: Maybe someone corrected you loudly after prayer. Maybe nobody said hello. Maybe you heard gossip, or saw a "good Muslim" act badly. If you've wondered, *"If this is Islam, do I want it?"*, today is for you.

**You're not imagining it, and you're not alone.** In ISPU focus groups, one of the biggest turn-offs at mosques for converts, young people and women was being "criticized, frowned upon, or rudely corrected" [ISPU RMS].
bubbles: And in a survey of 618 American converts, more than a third named intolerance from other Muslims as a source of doubt [Yaqeen 2025].

screens.text: **Islam is the measure. Muslims are people trying to meet it.** Some do it well, some badly, and all of us fall short sometimes.
bubbles: Sh. Abdullah Oduro, a convert who leads Yaqeen's convert work, puts it this way: separate the doer from the doctrine [Yaqeen DoubleTake].

screens.prompt: When a Muslim acts badly, what's the rule?
screens.answer: Judge the act by Islam, not Islam by the act
screens.feedback: That's it. Islam is the standard; a person's behavior is measured against it.

screens.title: What happened vs. what Islam teaches

cards.front: Someone laughed at how you pronounced the Arabic.
cards.back: The Qur'an forbids mocking others: they may be better than the mocker [Q 49:11]. You're the one following Islam here.

cards.front: Someone told everyone about a mistake you made.
cards.back: Islam forbids backbiting and prying into others' faults [Q 49:12].

cards.front: Nobody greeted you at the masjid.
cards.back: The Prophet ﷺ taught greeting both people you know and people you don't [Bukhari 12]. That's the standard, even when people miss it.

cards.front: Someone yelled at you for standing in the wrong spot.
cards.back: That isn't the Prophet's way ﷺ (next screen).

screens.text: **How the Prophet ﷺ corrected people.** A desert traveler once urinated inside the masjid. People rushed at him. The Prophet ﷺ told them to leave him alone, had the spot washed, and said: you were sent to make things easy, not hard [Bukhari 6128].
bubbles: Allah told him that if he had been harsh, people would have scattered from him [Q 3:159].
Gentleness is the Sunnah. Harshness isn't.

screens.situation: After Jumu'ah, a woman loudly tells Aaliyah her scarf is "wrong" in front of others. Aaliyah's face burns. On the drive home, she thinks, "I'm never going back."

options.text: Let herself be upset, tell her mentor, and go back next week, maybe sitting with someone she trusts
options.feedback: Yes. Her hurt is valid. One person's rudeness doesn't get to take her masjid or her faith.

options.text: Stop going to the masjid. The people there clearly aren't for her
options.feedback: Understandable, but not quite. One harsh person isn't the whole community, and isolation makes everything harder.

options.text: Decide that if Muslims act like this, maybe Islam isn't true
options.feedback: Not quite. That woman's behavior went against Islam [Q 49:11]. Judge the act by Islam, not Islam by the act.

screens.text: **Don't write off the whole community.** Most Muslims you'll meet are kind, and many are newer to their faith than they look. A bad moment is often ignorance, not malice.
bubbles: Find your people: the friendly few, your mentor, other converts.
If something is truly wrong (harassment, exploitation, abuse), tell {{mentor.name}} or the imam. Reporting harm isn't gossip.

items.text: Telling friends about an embarrassing mistake someone made
items.why: That spreads someone's faults, which Islam forbids [Q 49:12].

items.text: Telling the imam a man at the masjid keeps harassing you
items.why: Telling someone who can stop harm isn't gossip. Say it plainly and factually.

items.text: Telling {{mentor.name}} someone pressured you for money
items.why: Exploitation is harm. Your mentor needs to know so it can be stopped.

items.text: Joking in a group chat about how rude an uncle was
items.why: That's airing someone's faults for no fix [Q 49:12]. If it hurt you, tell your mentor instead.

screens.prompt: Has a Muslim hurt or disappointed you? Write what happened, how it felt, and what Islam actually says about it. Then: who's one Muslim who has shown you what the faith looks like at its best?

screens.text: Notice one Muslim who's been kind to you.
steps: Send a short thank-you to one Muslim who has been kind since you converted
screens.optional_extra: If something happened that still stings, tell {{mentor.name}} about it this week.

screens.text: Muslims are people; Islam is the standard. Judge the act by Islam, not Islam by the act, and keep finding the people who live it well.
Someone else's bad day doesn't get to decide your faith.

check.prompt: A Muslim mocks you at the masjid. What does Islam say about that?

options.text: Mocking others is forbidden. The mocker is the one going against Islam
options.feedback: Right. The Qur'an forbids ridiculing others [Q 49:11]. Judge the act by Islam.

options.text: It shows Islam allows people to be harsh
options.feedback: Not quite. Islam forbids mockery [Q 49:11], and the Prophet ﷺ corrected people gently [Bukhari 6128].

check.prompt: How did the Prophet ﷺ respond to the man who urinated in the masjid?

options.text: He stopped people from harming him and handled it gently
options.feedback: Right. He said we were sent to make things easy, not hard [Bukhari 6128].

options.text: He told everyone to throw him out
options.feedback: Not quite. He stopped the crowd, had the spot washed, and stayed gentle [Bukhari 6128].

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- ISPU's *Reimagining Muslim Spaces* focus groups (86 participants in DC, Detroit and the Bay Area) found being "criticized, frowned upon, or rudely corrected" at mosques was a major turn-off for young adults, women and converts [ISPU RMS; T1 Fact-Check Log #29–30: attribution confirmed, exact wording medium confidence].
- Yaqeen 2025 (n=618): intolerance of Muslims was a source of doubt for 37%; the report says converts' anguish comes overwhelmingly from Muslims' behavior, not doctrine [Yaqeen 2025].
- "Separate the doer from the doctrine": Sh. Abdullah Oduro on Yaqeen's DoubleTake podcast (V20).
- Islam forbids mockery [Q 49:11] and backbiting [Q 49:12]; greet those you know and don't [Bukhari 12]. The Prophet ﷺ handled the Bedouin gently: "you were sent to make things easy" [Bukhari 6128]. Harshness drives people away [Q 3:159].

**Likely questions**
- *"Someone was rude to me."* Validate first. Separate the act from Islam. Suggest telling the mentor, going back with a friend, and trying a different time or class. Don't attack the person.
- *"How can Muslims act like this if Islam is true?"* Muslims aren't Islam; every community has flawed people; the Qur'an itself warns believers against these behaviors, which shows they're wrong, not that Islam is. Take it seriously as a doubt (Day 33); never dismiss it.
- *"How do I report a problem?"* Telling the imam or mentor about harm, to fix it, isn't backbiting. Be factual. For anything involving abuse, exploitation or safety, use the safety rule.
- *"I don't feel welcome."* Ask what happened; suggest the mentor, convert groups, a different program or a nearby masjid; keep a path to community open.

**Escalate:** harassment, exploitation, financial or sexual misconduct, a mentor or leader behaving inappropriately (to the imam; and if the problem is the imam, to another staff member or a female staff member where requested); any danger (safety rule first).

**Don't**
- Don't trash the masjid, the community, any ethnic group or any named person.
- Don't tell the convert they're "too sensitive" or that they must tolerate mistreatment.
- Don't use this to argue that the convert's critic is a bad Muslim; focus on the act.
